title: The Fathers on Lamentations
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The multitude of people means the dwelling Israelites and the multitude of nations the proselytes, or in a higher sense the wealth of contemplations and the many good deeds.
comments.comment: And the multitude of the people, as far as the wording, seems to indicate the dwelling Israelites, and the multitude of the nations, as we said before, the proselytes. But unto anagogy—since the contemplative things are more kindred to the soul and less circumstantial than the practical—the wealth of contemplations; and the multitude of the nations the large number of good deeds. And after a little: She who was multiplied with people sits alone; by casting off the bridegroom Word the bride becomes as a widow who once was filled with the aforementioned nations (Lamentations 1:1).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem, once full of people and protected by the living Word as her husband, sits desolate and widowed because she sinned.
comments.comment: As far as the wording it fits for Jerusalem to be understood as said with amazement because of the change unto the gloomier—sitting isolated who once was full of people—so that the isolation may be her desolation, having had as husband the living Word as protector when she followed him present and helping, but widowed and left behind by him because of the things she had sinned. …
comments.selected_reason: Plain explanation of why the city sits alone.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In the higher sense Jerusalem is the divine soul, which can flourish and then, if it falls from the truth, be left alone, widowed and enslaved.
comments.comment: … These things then toward the literal; toward the sense, Jerusalem flourishing and full of people and nations and ruling countries is the divine soul. … And just as it is possible to see Jerusalem flourishing, multiplying with people and nations and ruling in countries, so—if virtue is liable to fall—sometimes seeing her isolated and widowed and enslaved, so as even to pay tributes to the enemy who has mastered her, according to the soul of the one who has fallen from the truth (Lamentations 1:1).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem pays tribute to Nebuchadnezzar for each of her stumbles, and to his satraps too.
comments.comment: And what need is there also to speak concerning this—that having begun to rule countries she is enslaved to such a degree among the enemies that she always also pays tribute, doing whatever those masters command? And they command nothing useful. And perhaps for each of the things in which she stumbles here she pays some tribute to Nebuchadnezzar, who is interpreted “Settling-in and recognition of constraint” (Lamentations 1:1); and not only to Nebuchadnezzar, but also to his satraps.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The city weeping in the night is the people reminded of how great a slavery they have fallen into, with none of those who loved her left to comfort them.
comments.comment:
… But upon this one what would someone say—a city being said to have wept in the night, so that the tears are upon her cheeks—unless perhaps someone will say that those named a city, who also pay tribute, have wept, having been reminded from what sort of peace and freedom into how great a slavery and humiliation they have come? How then shall we also narrate “in the night,” (Lamentations 1:2) or that in the time of the common rest of all human beings the city, being reminded, while resting wept, and wept with the tears flowing fountain-like upon their cheeks? And the wailing was most stretched out for them and the tears flowed on, there not being even one comforting them from so many who loved them, and everyone who loved setting aside the friendship toward her and having changed into enmity. Who then, as toward the wording, are those who formerly loved her, from whom there was not one who would comfort her? Perhaps the remaining cities of Judea—loving the metropolis for this reason—in a time of distress did not encourage her.

And after a little: These things then toward the literal. If the Word, as in the things before, should be said to weep—having fallen from her own country and coming to be in Confusion—and to have a condition opposite to laughing the laugh from joy and cheerfulness, which our Lord promises will belong to those who have wept the blessed weeping, saying: “Blessed are those who weep now, for they will laugh.” (Luke 6:21) And in Job also he says, “He will fill the mouth of the true ones with laughter.” (Job 8:21) And perhaps for this reason also one of the patriarchs is called Laughter. The one groaning, then—as also the apostle has made clear saying, “For indeed we who are in the tent groan, being burdened” (2 Corinthians 5:4)—weeps a weeping most nourishing and benefiting the soul, toward the cheerfulness in promise (2 Corinthians 5:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Loving is more divine than liking, so the better ones merely failed to comfort her while the lesser ones set her aside and became her enemies.
comments.comment: And we suppose that loving is more divine and, so to speak, spiritual, while liking is bodily and more human. And perhaps—since no base person loves—one must observe that concerning the better ones it says: “there is none comforting her from all who love her,” (Lamentations 1:2) but concerning the lesser: “all who like her have set her aside; they have become enemies to her.” For the more deficient both set her aside and became enemies to her; but the better ones only did not comfort.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judah left her high place through humiliation and long slavery to the passions, and among the nations she found no rest from her pursuers.
comments.comment: Toward the wording the sense would be such: Judea exchanged her own place, these things having become causes for her—her humiliation (in which she was humbled when she sinned and left behind the stature and the raised-up condition she formerly had while remaining in piety), and further also her much slavery, to which she had been enslaved when subjected to the passions. And having been relocated she settled among nations, where she has not been able to find rest, all the enemies pursuing her and overtaking and mastering her, she having come to be among the nations that were afflicting her (Lamentations 1:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The roads of Zion mourn when no one travels them, which in the sense of the soul means that the varied doctrines go unexamined once the contemplative power is captive to the passions.
comments.comment: And toward the sense: Zion being called the looking-out and contemplative power, there are many roads of the varied doctrines—mystical and physical and ethical, and perhaps also logical—that lead upon the understanding and vision of the things set forth. Whenever, then, someone, having lost the practiced habit of these, is thrown into confusion, all these roads mourn, not being traveled—there being a festival for the aforementioned roads when they are traveled, examined and, so to speak, crossed through; but they mourn when they are desolated, not being researched nor journeyed through because those traveling have fallen away and, having been taken captive by the passions, have been distracted about the worse things (Lamentations 1:4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zion has nothing sweet and lives in bitterness, not anger.
comments.comment: Zion, having nothing sweet at all, lives through bitterness by herself; for one must not take “being embittered” (Lamentations 1:4) now of some form of anger.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ways of Zion mourn because no one hurries to the festival any more and the gates have been torn down.
comments.comment: … The prophet Jeremiah, being utterly devastated, says in the book of Lamentations: 'The ways of Zion mourn because no one comes to the festival; all her gates are destroyed, and her priests groan' (Lam 1:4-5). For how could the ways of Zion not mourn, having been deprived of those walking, with no one still hurrying for the sake of celebrating and making a festival in Jerusalem, and the gates being destroyed, torn away by those who seized them tyrannically? …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Enemies who could not prevail while God shielded the Jews became their masters once the Jews sinned and killed the prophets, and God humbled them for their many impieties.
comments.comment: The clarity of the wording is somehow such. Certain ones were afflicting the Judean country—or at least wanted to afflict—before the times of the captivity, but they did not master while God was shielding the Jews, when those were rendering themselves worthy of help. But when they sinned and, in addition to not hearing the prophets, the sons of Israel were even killing them, then they were handed over subject to the afflictors, so that their enemies became head—that is, as Symmachus interpreted, rulers. And others, perhaps besides the afflictors, being enemies either in conception or also in substance, were in prosperity, those abandoned because of the sins having become subject to the afflictors—the Lord having humbled the lawbreakers because of the multitude of the impieties, and having done this to such a degree that not even for their infants was mercy left, but that they went in captivity, driven by every afflictor (Lamentations 1:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The enemies ruled and rejoiced because the Lord humbled the covenant-breakers.
comments.comment: Both having ruled and having rejoiced because the Lord, on account of the multitude of the impieties, handed over unto humiliation those who had not kept the covenants with him in the holy oracles (Lamentations 1:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The daughter of Zion is the synagogue, her comeliness was carried off by plunderers, and her rulers, like rams without pasture, were led away weak.
comments.comment: The things of the wording, as far as power is ours, must be clarified, as we examine who the daughter of Zion is, and in what she has the comeliness, and what the pasture is which the rulers of the daughter of Zion do not have—like rams at a loss for grazing—and how these, deprived of strength, walk before the face of the pursuer. And we hold that the mountain Zion is mother of the synagogue in it, the synagogue being named daughter of Zion; and the comeliness of the daughter of Zion the possession in her robes, which possession, taken by the enemies in the time of the plundering, went out from those of whom it was adornment—that is, was carried out (for more emphatically he named this with “went out” (Lamentations 1:6)); and the leaders of the synagogue, because the enemies were pressing and taking captive, being at a loss for the customary things, have been likened to rams not finding food. Just as rams driven without having been fed walk weakly, yielding to the necessity of those pursuing, so also the rulers, having become captives, being led away into the country of those who took them captive, were walking not in strength before the sight of the pursuer.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In the soul's sense the daughter of Zion is the contemplative soul, whose adornment is the wealth of holy doctrines and whose leaders, like rams without pasture, fall to the pursuer when she neglects it.
comments.comment: And toward the sense, such a soul is daughter of Zion: just as the just woman is daughter of righteousness and the wise woman child of wisdom, so—since Zion is the Lookout—the looking-out and theoretically traversing soul would be called daughter of Zion. And what else would I rightly suppose her comeliness and dignity to be than the wealth of the holy doctrines of the truth contemplated with wisdom? Whenever, then, after acquiring comeliness and dignity, someone neglects both the holding-together of these and the increase of the divine wealth, the things that until then were her adornment flow away and go out. And rulers—those who led the word and guided unto the acquisition of the aforementioned comeliness—like rams that led the flock of sheep and do not find pasture, have themselves also stood in scarcity, having let go the attention of the things able to fatten, so to speak, both them and the sheep. For this reason, having grown weak, having been overtaken by the pursuer—who is our adversary the devil—they walk before him, driven wherever that one wishes to lead. If, however, the aforementioned daughter of Zion takes care of her beauty and her comeliness and foresight that the dignity be guarded, she despises and sneers at the king of the Assyrians, as we have learned from Isaiah saying: “The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and sneered at you.” (Lamentations 1:6) (Isaiah 37:22)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem remembers her past humiliation and rejections once her people have fallen into an afflictor's hand with no helper, and grasps her sins as the cause.
comments.comment: For the one remembering while suffering such-and-such things does not remember the present, but the past. … Having raised such difficulties in the place and seeking a reminder of her past humiliation and of her rejections—because her people have fallen into a hand of an afflictor and the things brought upon her have come about—we consider whether perhaps humiliation in the proper sense is nothing other than sin, just as exaltation is right practice, and rejection comes about from nothing operating except base action; for this is sufficient to thrust away from God and from everything finest according to nature. When, then, Jerusalem was drunk—that is, those dwelling in her—and beside herself from the sin she was being humbled, she was not delighted in the stumbles; but when her repayments have come through her people having fallen into hands of the afflictor, no one helping her, then she was reminded of the things because of which she was suffering, grasping those as causes both of her people’s having fallen and of her having been left helpless. … And if such a soul is Jerusalem, it is worthwhile to seek her people, upon whose falling into a hand of an afflictor—because there is no helper—she herself remembers the days of her humiliation, and still also of her own rejections by which she was rejected, and besides also of her desirable things, as many as were from ancient days. And see whether the contemplations in the knowing soul are not the people of Jerusalem, which, because the soul has come to be in inattention and neglect, falls, being thrown down by every afflictor. For the doctrines of those neglecting flow away, being squeezed out by the sins that have gained room in the one neglecting the better things, in no way having the help from the Word (Lamentations 1:7).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Jerusalem sinned she fell into tossing and dishonor from those who once glorified her, and, groaning, she stopped going forward into sins and drew back.
comments.comment: The sense of the wording is such. Because Jerusalem sinned a sin, she has come to be in tossing and confusion to such a degree that all who formerly glorified her, having changed, have dishonored such a city, having beheld her shame. And she herself, for the things she has suffered because of the sins—having fallen into tossing and into dishonor from those who once glorified her—groaning, has no longer gone forward into the sins, but having lessened them has withdrawn backward. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A soul that falls out of virtue and lives with wickedness is soundly said to be in tossing.
comments.comment: … And if such a soul is called Jerusalem—one skilled and sharp-sighted and able to understand the peace of God that surpasses every mind—since it is possible for many causes for this one to sin, it is shown that she has fallen over into tossing, having stood away from the good things and having come to be among the worse. And everyone who has fallen out of virtue and lives with wickedness is soundly said to be in tossing (Lamentations 1:8) (Philippians 4:7).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel was not handed over by chance but for earlier sins, and 'sinned a sin' stresses how great the sin was.
comments.comment: … often an anger and a plague that comes upon someone shows that person's sin. He [Israel] endured much impiety, and was delivered to the Assyrians, and to the Babylonians into their hand; for it did not happen that the handing over of Israel occurred by chance, but because of sins previously committed; 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin' (Lamentations 1:8), and it became a reproach. He sinned much sin, and not simply he sinned, but also 'a sin': 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin'. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jerusalem's sins were cut short as she turned back to her own good.
comments.comment: It shows the cutting-short of Jerusalem’s sins—she no longer stretching forward unto the former stumbles nor coming to be in the advance of the sins, but turning away backward upon her own good (Lamentations 1:8) (Philippians 3:13).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem's uncleanness hindered her journey, and because she did not remember her last things she lowered her great things into lowliness and had no comforter.
comments.comment: According to the bodily narrative what is said about Jerusalem now is such. Uncleanness is an obstacle for Jerusalem; but of what it is an obstacle, the prophet has left for us to understand. Perhaps it shows that the uncleanness is a hinderer of her journey. And also, being such, it shows that Jerusalem did not remember her last things. And the one who has these before the eyes and sees what will meet him because of the sins will not sin. Because of this uncleanness, then, there is an obstacle for her; and because she does not remember her last things, she brought down her wonderful and great things—which she had when she was worthy to be overseen—and led them into lowliness, though formerly they were oversized and greater than every praise. But also after all these things there was none comforting her: “See, O Lord, my humiliation,” (Lamentations 1:9) says the speaker, “since the enemy is magnified over what has happened to my homeland.” (Lamentations 1:9) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In the higher sense the soul's uncleanness hinders walking the holy road and must be washed off by Jesus, as he washed the disciples' feet.
comments.comment: … Yet one must inquire, according to the laws of the ascent-sense, whether it is possible for uncleanness to be in someone who is not its cause. And let us also see the first thoughts of the Lament. Such a soul, having fallen away, is altogether also in uncleanness, which uncleanness hinders walking the holy road. And just as holy Moses and his successor Joshua are commanded by God to loose the sandals when stepping upon a holy place—it not being fitting for the feet to wear dead hide in a holy place—so if someone is going to walk unimpeded, perhaps he ought not only to loose but also to wash off the uncleanness that has come about from the dust around the feet. And we suppose a symbol of this to be that the Savior, having put water into the basin, washed the feet of the disciples, saying to Peter who did not yet understand the mystery and for this reason was hindering: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me,” (John 13:8) and “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know after these things.” (John 13:7) Therefore it will be necessary for the uncleanness around the feet of the soul, so to speak, also to need Jesus, so that he may wash it off and we may be able to have a part with him. For if this remains, it is an obstacle to our walking the road according to the sound word—the Savior who said: “I am the way.” (John 14:6)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The healthy soul looks ahead, refusing a present sweetness that brings later bitterness and accepting present roughness for the sweet things that follow.
comments.comment: And it is clear that the healthy soul—or at least the one wanting to be such—does these things, not looking so much at the present alone as foreseeing what also unto the future will meet from the things being accomplished. And if, something thought useful coming to be for the present, she foresees the bitterness in the future, dismissing what seems to be sweet she does the opposite, for the sake of not later falling into something hard; and if, the present being toilsome, good hopes succeed what appears harsh, she will voluntarily give herself over to the roughness of what would seem terrible to some, for the sake of attaining the sweet things that succeed the harsh ones because of having endured these (Lamentations 1:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Having turned from the Word within her, the soul loses her comforter, and the cry 'See, O Lord, my humiliation' can be said by a kinsman of the soul or by the Word dishonored in her.
comments.comment: And all these things, it says, the one more tropically called Jerusalem having suffered, she did not even have abundance of the one comforting; for having turned away from the Word in her and having become wholly of the passion, she has lost the helper—the one who always arms the disposition that attends to him against the pains and against the things thought terrible. And upon these things see my humiliation—me the citizen; as a kinsman of a soul would say: the passion of my fellow-citizen, because of the love of humanity in which I was taught, is my calamity. Understand, then, O Lord, and do not utterly leave the one who has suffered the things said before; do not overlook the enemy against her—I mean wickedness magnified and poured out against her. And more tropically “See, O Lord, my humiliation” (Lamentations 1:9) can be said by the Word existing in the soul, having been dishonored and humbled and, so to speak, having lost its own kingdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The desirable things of Jerusalem are the things stored in the temple, such as the golden lampstand, which the people valued above all, and 'sanctuary' is the circumcision's name for the temple.
comments.comment: Desirable things of Jerusalem, then, must be understood as the things in the temple, and the things laid away in the holy of holies for the priestly liturgy, and the things otherwise believed to be divine by being stored in the temple—for example the golden lampstand and the rest. For those from the people, persuaded that these are stored in the temple unto the glory of God, preferred them above all, themselves wanting rather to suffer something hard from the enemies than for any of these to become subject to the enemies. And “sanctuary” (Lamentations 1:10) is a custom for those from the circumcision to call the temple.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Groaning from famine, the people gave the most honorable things they had left for a little food, since the enemy took what he wanted and left the rest.
comments.comment: They were groaning because of famine, and for the sake of a small bit of food that turns back a failing soul they were giving over the most honorable things. And how were they giving the aforementioned desirable things—carried off by the enemies—unto purchase of food? But “the enemy stretched out the hand upon all,” (Lamentations 1:10) and having been filled by taking what he wanted, he left the rest; in exchange for which they bought the food.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem prays 'See, O Lord, my dishonor' and, like Esau giving up his birthright for red food, gave her desirable things for food, as a soul throws away divine lessons for necessities.
comments.comment: A prayer from Jerusalem: “See, O Lord, my dishonor,” (Lamentations 1:11) she who has lost the adornment because of famine. And perhaps the desirable things are different—primarily the ones shown before “upon which the enemy stretched out the hand,” (Lamentations 1:10) and secondarily those of each one from the people; and the common ones he took, but in exchange for the private ones each was buying food. And toward the ascent-sense: just as Esau gave away the birthrights for the sake of red food, of which he has become namesake—Edom, that is Red earth; for he also became earthy, having despised the birthrights and having made the earthly things primary, which Jacob pursued as necessary in a secondary account because of being in a body—so also Jerusalem. But the one gives to worthy Jacob to obtain what desirable things he had, even if he did not choose these first; and the people of Jerusalem also gave for the sake of food, but not of a holy one preparing this, but of Babylonians who were going to insult the desirable things given. For Jacob knows how to adorn the things from Esau, but the Babylonians do not use the things given unto their own good. So also a soul, through lack of the necessary needs, throws away the divine lessons to those who from curiosity want to learn unto slander and mockery.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fire and the nets show the burning at the capture and the seizure into slavery of those who did not use freedom well, so the city fell into continual grief.
comments.comment: He has shown the burning at the capture that touched the strongest buildings, or the capture of the outstanding citizens in her, being as it were fired in soul and in the outward things by the calamities. It also shows the seizure of those below unto slavery as in a catch of nets—of those who did not use freedom well. For these, not stretching forward unto the things ahead of the things behind, were turning away from glory unto dishonor, from freedom unto slavery, and have become, instead of glorious ones, dimmed and unseen from dishonor and insolence; because of which the city has fallen into continual grief (Lamentations 1:13) (Philippians 3:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God has taken Jerusalem's impieties into his hands and woven them into works of repayment, so they lie on her like a yoke.
comments.comment: Providence, she says, has not slept over my impieties; for God, as if taking them into hands through examination, has woven them into the works that are for repayment. And these have become for me just as a yoke upon a neck and have set slavery; for the slavery I served to Nebuchadnezzar is my impieties, for which reason I have become without tension, having been handed over to those whose mastery I cannot endure. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The yoke and the hand of God must be taken tropically, for a soul that threw off the saving yoke is bound by the yoke of impieties, which as conscience chokes and prevents lifting the head.
comments.comment: … “His yoke is upon my neck.” (Lamentations 1:14) And through the present saying it is shown that one must take more tropically the things said as about our passions concerning God. For how else have the impieties of Jerusalem been woven with the hand of God, except tropically? For no one would say these things also bodily. And how is it not out of place, Jerusalem being a city, for the neck to be taken tropically, but the members spoken of as of God not to be heard in the same manner? And let the present things be said as by a soul that has fallen asleep unto impiety, in having thrown off the saving yoke of the sound word—which the Savior names kind—and having slipped under the yoke of the impieties, through which she grew weak, having been left of the divine oversight and handed over to sin that reigns among the evils, whose wills, because of the unbounded and infinite character of wickedness, she cannot altogether serve and provide satiety. And truly sin humbles and chokes and makes one look downward; and a yoke also is the conscience, always choking and wounding and not allowing one to lift the head and stripping away all boldness of speech. And a paresis, she says, of the strength which I used not well, he has made, and I am loosed as I behold the evils that hold me together (Matthew 11:30) (Romans 6:12–14).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God condemned my strong and chosen ones to suffer in my midst because of my impiety, trampling the winepress of his wrath, as the cup of the Psalms is poured from one sinner to another.
comments.comment: He did not take them up out of my midst (for even if I had been deprived of them, it was still possible to use them for other things), but in my midst he condemned them to suffer because of the things in which I was impious, and my chosen ones have suffered the harshest things—the Lord himself having trampled the wine of his wrath in a winepress unto fullness for me and for the virgin of most-kingly Judah. And he would call “strong” (Lamentations 1:15) those powerful in war and shielding the homeland, and “chosen” the well-born or wise. And “he trampled a winepress” clarifies what is said in the Psalms about the punishment of sinners: “a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed mixture,” (Psalm 75:8) being tipped from this one being punished upon that one being punished, until “all the sinners of the earth” drink, the lees being left for those still more sinful than these, into whom last “the lees” will be emptied.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul, deprived through wickedness of the strong and chosen gifts her Creator gave her, confesses her suffering and is benefited by mourning, which brings the promise of comfort.
comments.comment: The soul, then, having received from the one who created her many strong and chosen gifts, having been deprived of these through wickedness and paying penalties, confesses what she has suffered. And the time called unto being crushed is the time of repayment, when according to Ezekiel all the righteous deeds which the righteous one has done will not be remembered in a day of sin. And mourning the things that have befallen she is benefited—those who mourn and weep having the promise of comfort and of laughter (Lamentations 1:15) (Ezekiel 18:24) (Matthew 5:4) (Luke 6:21).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zion laments that no one turns her soul back, and the sons have vanished because the enemy is empowered by our sins and is weak when we are pious.
comments.comment: She said the cause of the lamentations to be that there is none turning her soul back—or, according to Symmachus, reclaiming it. And she says the sons also have vanished, the enemy having been empowered through the things in which they were sinning; for when we are pious he does not prevail—for he is weak when we advance, and is put to death when we are perfected, and is crushed under the feet, being made fine as dust before the face of wind, and as mud of streets being made fine. For analogously to the things in which we sin he is fed and gains power; but when we have ceased from stumbling he is as it were destroyed by famine. And from the opposites: when we do well we strengthen the divine powers for ourselves, and when we sin we chase them away. For which reason Symmachus instead of “vanished” (Lamentations 1:16) rendered “deserted.” (Psalm 18:42) And a contemplative soul would say these things—being of the Word of the truth and through slackness having lost this gladdening Word and all the fruits that are named her sons—because wickedness hostile against her has been empowered (Lamentations 1:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zion is the mountain, Jacob the people and Jerusalem the mother-city, and Jacob was surrounded for transgressing the commandments.
comments.comment: Zion, she says, is the mountain, and Jacob the people, and Jerusalem the mother-city. And God commanded to Jacob commandments through which, being transgressed, he was surrounded by enemies; and according to Symmachus and according to another edition of the Seventy, the Lord commanded those afflicting him to come to be round about him—to the powers arranged unto harming (Lamentations 1:17).
comments.selected_reason: Identifies Zion, Jacob and Jerusalem and says why the enemies surround Jacob.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem's uncleanness through sin is like menstruation, and Zion's hands are spread out and idle from the works of farming and handwork, so the whole mountain and nation groan with no comforter.
comments.comment: He has shown the uncleanness of Jerusalem through sin as through menstruation. And “in the midst” (Lamentations 1:17) he says either of Zion and of Jacob, or of the whole mountain (for she has been built in a part of it) and of the whole people—Jacob now signifying the twelve scepters. And twofold according to the wording one can take Zion and Jerusalem: either the places or the inhabitants. But if Zion is a place, her hands are the works—for example farming and whatever is handmade—he says spread out and not drawn together nor doing the fitting work with hands, as in an idle and deserted country. And if he means the inhabitants, hands would be farmers and workers, not drawing the hands together unto works because of the things that have surrounded. And if the hands of Zion are tropologized, how much more the members of God according to the scripture. And the mountain itself, so to speak, with the nation groans, having for comfort neither God nor a holy man.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Virgins and young men are the holy who suffer with the guilty.
comments.comment: After the perceptible: understand virgins as those living in incorruption, and young men as those well-approved in virtue. For often even the holy ones suffer with those liable (Lamentations 1:18).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lament speaks of things that have already befallen the city, a personification, so no literal womb or loosed heart is to be sought.
comments.comment: In the prophecy, then, he grieves in soul as one about to suffer most terrible things; but in the present Lament, as these things having already befallen, he is weighed down and through sins confesses that the kindness of God has set herself most bitter—so as even for the many-childed to be made childless, and the most terrible thing, by a hostile hand. And there being a personification, one must not seek a city’s womb that has given birth and a heart that has been loosed (Lamentations 1:20).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem says she was left to suffer so that the nations might be saved, and with the one for whom the promises were laid up now come, no one still comforts her.
comments.comment: Jerusalem divides the word toward the enemies, whom she wants to hear, and toward God. But why does she call the enemies unto hearing? And what does she say to God about them—as that they rejoiced? Perhaps, then, since by her and Israel’s stumbling the salvation has come to be for the nations unto making them jealous, and when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved—toward those from the nations she speaks the first things prophetically, and toward God the second. I have been left to suffer so that you may receive room, and I have become because of you an enemy of God, though according to the election beloved because of the fathers. Therefore, having heard my groaning, understand also the cause of this; for completely unto your salvation I have been left behind, not having the one always comforting me after trial of evils. For now a ruler has failed from Judah, and a leader from the thighs; for he has come for whom the things laid away were, the expectation of the nations—whose blood being avenged, there is no longer anyone comforting Jerusalem (Lamentations 1:21) (Romans 11:11) (Romans 11:25–28) (Genesis 49:10).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prayer asks that their wickedness come under God's oversight, as wounds come to a physician for healing.
comments.comment: That is: let their wickedness not still more be left free to use, but let it come to be in your oversight—as if someone should pray that wounds come into sight of a physician toward obtaining complete healing; for this is the “all.” (Lamentations 1:22) For most blessed is first not to sin, and second that all our wickedness be overseen by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Gleaning is gathering what is left after the vintage, and Jerusalem asks God to cleanse her enemies as he cleansed her branches.
comments.comment: And “to glean” (Lamentations 1:22) is after vintage to gather the small things of what was left, which the poor do. Just as, then, when you were overseeing carefully, you were cleansing my branches, taking away all the worse things even unto the smallest—of the grape and of the cluster of bitterness—so do this to my enemies; for this profits me, if after they have been completely saved I too according to your judgment, O Lord, will obtain salvation; whom seeing I have both been greatly pained and condemned myself, needing the oversight from you (Deuteronomy 32:32).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The footstool that the Lord did not remember is the ancient temple.
comments.comment: … And the ancient temple is also called his footstool, as it is written in Jeremiah: 'How the Lord in his wrath darkened the daughter of Zion! He cast down to the earth her sanctuary; he did not remember his footstool' (Lam 2:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God punishes as an enemy not from hostility but to benefit those suffering or seeing, and the tent is the temple and the bow his punishing power.
comments.comment: For even in the temple the enemies dared the slaughters, God permitting. And well the “as an enemy” (Lamentations 2:4); for God does not punish as being hostile, but wanting to benefit either those suffering or those seeing. And he calls the temple a tent according to the sanctuary from the beginning, and a bow the punishing power as in Habakkuk: “stretching you will stretch your bow upon the scepters, says the Lord” (Habakkuk 3:9)—clearly the opposing rulers and authorities. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son, God's right hand, destroyed the idols in the temple and killed the demons in them.
comments.comment: … And the Son, being right hand of God and Father, strongly contended, having also destroyed the idols which they set in the temple of God (for these are desire of eyes), having killed instead of the idols the demons that settled in (Ephesians 6:12) (1 John 2:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Palaces are houses, which Symmachus called kingdoms; in the soul's sense the houses are virtues and the fortifications irrefutable reasonings.
comments.comment: “Palaces” (Lamentations 2:5) he says for the houses, which Symmachus rendered “kingdoms.” And he takes up the laments again, as someone greatly pained upon mourning. And again he shows that she has taken on a lowly reckoning and a lowly thought, the things like houses and fortresses having been taken down, as filling the leading part. For virtues are the houses—for by them we are sheltered—and fortifications the irrefutable reasonings. For the demolition now is not of worse heights, “lifting themselves up against the knowledge of God,” (Lamentations 2:5) nor of lowliness according to which one “learns the judgments of God”; for these are of a character for joy, not for grief.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The tent is the temple and the vineyard Israel, whose fence God removed by handing his guard over to the enemies, and he abolished the appointed feasts and provoked king and priest.
comments.comment: Tent he calls the temple, and vine and vineyard Israel according to “a vine from Egypt you removed” (Psalm 80:8) in David, and “a vineyard came to be for the beloved” (Isaiah 5:1) in Isaiah. And David adds: “why did you take down its fence?” (Psalm 80:12) and what follows; and Isaiah: “you removed its fence” (Isaiah 5:5) and the things upon this. These things the present Lament also has shown. For God, having drawn together his own guard, handed them over to the enemies, no longer encamping round about him because of not fearing the Lord. And he has also abolished the times according to law unto worship, as in Isaiah he says: “fast and rest and your feasts my soul hates” (Isaiah 1:14)—which he called a forgetting, but not as a human passion. And he provoked king and priest, being indignant if, being a portion of God, they undergo such things from the impious (Lamentations 2:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God took her security, stretching out the measure of punishment.
comments.comment: For he has taken away all her security, having stretched out the measure of the punishment—which indeed Zechariah also has seen (Lamentations 2:8) (Zechariah 2:1–2).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gates sank and king, rulers, false prophets and law perished, and in the soul the gates are the senses, flooded by passions, until she becomes Babylon, full of Confusion.
comments.comment: For as if swallowed by earth or sea they have become unseen. And king and rulers and the false prophets have also perished, and her law by necessity of slavery—which indeed by choice even before being captured they had dissolved. And gates of a soul are the senses, which when she sins are both flooded by passions and become earthy. And the powers of the soul that keep these also are loosed, when mind that rules and ruling reasonings have perished in the passions—when both law and order of the soul are destroyed and she becomes Babylon, being full of Confusion, having nothing providential helped by God (Lamentations 2:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Fear kept even the elders from lamenting and made the first virgins look to the earth, and in the soul the elders in virtue become earthy and settled in passions.
comments.comment: He narrates painful sights that have come to be in the place of gladness; for by fear they were not permitting even the elders to lament, and they prepared the first virgins to look unto the earth, lest appearing they draw them by force from the beauty in which they were foremost. And you would also say those long ago elders in virtue—for which they were so called—having become earthy and settled in irrational passions, still do nothing according to reason, and having made earthy the leading spirit in them and having made the sobriety they once had worthy of mourning and having corrupted reasonings which formerly they were keeping incorrupt (Lamentations 2:10).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet calls the temple and his country's piety his own glory, and he makes the sufferings of his kin his own, as Paul says 'who is weak, and I am not weak?'
comments.comment: The prophet calls his own glory both temple of God and piety of homeland. And the famine was working the fainting of the infants. And you would say more loftily that he makes his own the passions of those kindred according to flesh according to “who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Corinthians 11:29)—taking up those difficult things according to their soul: a withering of true knowledge and an unstable bearing of the reasoning toward the earthly things and a deprivation of that which lifts the head according to “you, O Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one lifting my head.” (Lamentations 2:11) (Psalm 3:3)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The passion is so great that prophets could not heal it, so God alone, who struck, will heal.
comments.comment: He has shown the complete wickedness, as having no witness of virtue at all, nor anyone who has stumbled in similar things. For what sin is like that of the one far from God and of the one who after drawing near has thrown off the reins? For “if I had not come,” (John 15:22) he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” (John 15:22) For which reason also “among those who draw near to me I will be sanctified” (Leviticus 10:3); because the one who does not know the will of the Lord and does not do it will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knows and does not do it will be beaten with many. The passion so great, then, which prophets have not been able to heal, needs God alone. For which reason he has also worn flesh—the prophets confessing weakness in “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isaiah 53:1) And formerly Jerusalem was also saying: “See if there is a passion according to my passion.” (Lamentations 1:12) The one who struck, then, will heal—“for he himself makes to suffer and again restores.” (Job 5:18) The “who” is taken both of the rare and of the none; for no human being can heal the blow brought on by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no one but God can heal her.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Vain prophecy has no outcome and comes from idols and from those who prophesy for barley and bread, while true oracles join to God by thrusting out error.
comments.comment: Vain prophecy is that which has no outcome and which vain idols prepare. And from themselves some were prophesying, forsooth, “for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread” (Ezekiel 13:19) according to what is written—who do not know how to reprove sins and to save from the captivity under demons, twisting the souls through smooth speech. And just as of the true ones the oracle and the word which they receive from God is by nature true and joins to God, so that of the demons is both false and distancing from God and thrust out from the inclination from there. And what are the thrustings-out that are not vain, just as has been shown, and the oracles? Clearly those that thrust out error and lead toward God (Lamentations 2:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what makes the prophecy vain and what true oracles do.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wall here is the king, rulers and defenders, who are told to weep repentance, and the people are told to weep night and day, for repentance leads to salvation, and to keep the mind joined to Christ.
comments.comment: There are times when scripture makes the words full of feeling and gives perception to the unperceiving, introducing hills leaping and mountains skipping, and calling hills and stones to witness; which in these things is impossible, the wall having already been taken down by enemies. Wall here, then, is both king and rulers and as many as by power were walling her round—whom he counts worthy to pour unceasing tears of repentance, which the fallen wall throughout procures for those who see. These things, he says, belong to them—even if again he signifies the grief of the power that long ago was guarding, showing this hyperbolically. “And in affliction,” he says, “they remembered the Lord from their whole heart.” (Lamentations 2:18) Do this, then, he says, weeping night and day and “on your beds be pricked” (Psalm 4:4); and do not consider release from these things to be sobriety; for repentance is unto salvation. And one is sober not by ceasing from good things, but from worse ones. And join the mind continually toward Christ, so that he may guard you as pupil of an eye and may become a wall for you (2 Corinthians 7:10) (Deuteronomy 32:10).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Lift your hands to God by good works, for your infants are failing for lack of the divine Word.
comments.comment: Lift your hands toward him through the working of the good things. The contest is not about chance matters—your infants failing through lack of the divine Word and standing upon the beginning of all the ways out, of the commandments of God, and not able to advance without God’s cooperation and of the bread that strengthens the heart (Lamentations 2:19) (Psalm 104:15).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem, persuaded by the prophet, prays for mercy, admits she took the Law's threats of eating her children for mere words, and says she had not heard of priest and prophet slain in the sanctuary.
comments.comment: The prophet having exhorted, Jerusalem was persuaded and says toward God: “do not turn your face away from me,” (Psalm 27:9) “look upon me and have mercy on me,” (Psalm 25:16) “do not convict me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger.” (Psalm 6:1) The blow is greater than human nature. I know I transgressed the law and the penalties from there in which is also “you will eat the offspring of your belly, flesh of your sons and your daughters.” (Leviticus 26:29) I was thinking the words were as far as a threat; Lord, that “your law is truth.” (Psalm 119:142) And I had not heard of a slaughter of priest and prophet in the midst of a sanctuary (Lamentations 2:20).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Young men and virgins lay slain on the ground, and the exits of earth are the affairs of life in which they slept, not staying awake or praying.
comments.comment: Upon the earth were thrown all who through age were unable toward the toils—a sight exceedingly pitiable—as also a slaughter of young men and of virgins; would that even of these there were slaughters before being led away unto a more bitter life. And exits of earth are the affairs of life, in which they slept, not having stayed awake nor prayed, but having also closed in folly the eyes of the soul. And who are these? If children, not very amazing. But now before these, those seeming to have advanced according to virtue, and everyone incorrupt in soul and powerful in war, has become subject to enemies. You as good put such a life of theirs to rest, and you cut down every constitution of theirs unto evil (Lamentations 2:21) (Matthew 26:41).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Her neighbors in Judea thought the feast a refuge, but none are left because of God's wrath.
comments.comment: Those dwelling round about me, she says, in Judea were thinking the feast unto me a refuge, hoping salvation from there; of whom none has been left because of your wrath brought upon them. For through the things in which I sinned, the enemies have become many and powerful (Lamentations 2:22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Beginning another alphabet, the prophet bewails himself, seeing the city's poverty and desolation, for he too lacked good things, shared their calamities from sympathy and was mocked all day.
comments.comment: Terrible things have befallen the prophet both before the city was taken and when this had been captured. For which reason, beginning another alphabetic sequence, he bewails himself, seeing poverty and desolation of the city through the Lord’s discipline. And he himself no less has come to be in lack of good things—at once having come to be in circumstance when he was convicting these, so as to say “I continued being mocked the whole day,” (Jeremiah 20:7) and at once also sharing in the calamities of their terrible things and from sympathy. And he also says according to David: “a shadow of death overshadowed me.” (Psalm 44:19) For when he seems for a short while to give relief to the pains, again he runs back making continuous punishment (Lamentations 3:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sin has brought rottenness.
comments.comment: It signifies the rottenness that has befallen us from the sin (Lamentations 3:4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Lasting calamity ages us.
comments.comment: For a persistent calamity produces an old man’s weakness (Lamentations 3:4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God has surrounded him with inescapable evils and a heavy burden, and his prayer was not heard, for God had told him not to pray for them.
comments.comment: He has surrounded me with inescapable evils, having set upon my neck a harsh and embittering people and a burden greater than according to me. And I was not heard to be lightened, though having prayed many times; for circumstances sometimes prevent the holy ones from being heard. And he would also mean a yoke and the iron collars, which instead of wooden ones by God’s command he put around himself; for a writing is also current: “for he made heavy the bronze of my neck.” (Lamentations 3:7–8) For he blocked my prayer also having said to him: “do not pray about them; for I will not hear you.” (Jeremiah 28:13) (Jeremiah 7:16)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God emptied every arrow against him, wounding his desire.
comments.comment: Every arrow of his, he says, he emptied against me, wounding my desire and not allowing me to act as I wish (Lamentations 3:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Struck on the cheek and eating ash as bread, he could not be at peace within or without, and having hoped nothing useful he uttered Job's words.
comments.comment: With a pebble, he says, or by number—being struck upon the cheek according to each tooth—or with a hard stone. And according to David he also says: “I was eating ash as my bread,” (Psalm 102:9) showing that he was not even taking bread with pleasure because of affliction. It was not possible, then, for the soul to be in peace—herself being troubled and moreover seeing outward tumults, inward fights. For which reason, having hoped nothing useful, I uttered Job’s voices: “mercy has renounced me, and my hope from the Lord.” (Lamentations 3:16–18) For it was not possible to conquer the surrounding terrors (Job 6:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, though good to all, requires our endurance, so the soul seeking him must wait undisturbed until his mercy meets her, without prying into the judgments of providence.
comments.comment: For being good toward all he requires the endurance from us. For for the soul that will seek him, the seeking is good—she who would endure undisturbed until the mercy should meet, and not removing until the Lord’s salvation should appear, unto hoping unto another. And perhaps “and he will be quiet” (Lamentations 3:25–26) means not being busybody about the judgments of providence. One must, then, even if we are ignorant, not throw off the Lord’s reins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old writings too know the saying to offer the other cheek, since Lamentations says a man bearing a yoke in his youth will give his cheek to the one who strikes him.
comments.comment:
[Answering Celsus:] … the old writings too know the saying “To the one who strikes you on the right cheek, offer the other also” (Matthew 5:39). At any rate, it is written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent, because he has taken it upon himself. He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, and he will be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:27–28, 30).

The Gospel of God does not issue orders contrary to the God of the Law, not even about the blow on the cheek taken literally. Neither of the two is lying, neither Moses nor Jesus; nor did the Father, in sending Jesus, forget what he had commanded Moses; nor indeed did he condemn his own laws, change his mind, and send his messenger for the opposite purpose.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the good, and not the evil, comes forth from the Lord's mouth, for God made all things very good.
comments.comment: … God has made all things 'very good' (Gen 1:31). 'From the mouth of the Lord neither the good nor the evil shall come forth' (Lamentations 3:38). He does not say that neither the good nor the evil, but rather that the good shall come forth from the mouth of the Lord, and the evil not. Thus, the good are in the plural. For this reason, there is no place for the evil among the existing things; for God has made all things 'very good.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evils are not from God, as Jeremiah shows, and matter is not their cause, for the ruling part of each person is the cause of the vice in it.
comments.comment:
Then, as though he had something more secret to say about the origin of evils but kept silent about it and said only what suits the multitude, he says that it is enough to say to the multitude about the origin of evils that “evils are not from God, but cling to matter and have their home among mortals.”

Now it is true that evils are not from God. For according to our Jeremiah too it is plain that “out of the mouth of the Lord will not come forth evil things and the good” (Lamentations 3:38). But it is not true, in our view, that matter, having its home among mortals, is the cause of evils. For the ruling part of each person is the cause of the vice that exists in it, and this vice is what is evil; and the actions that come from it are evils too. And in our view, speaking strictly, nothing else is evil.

But I know that this subject needs much working out and proof. These can come, by the grace of God who enlightens the ruling part, to the one whom God has judged worthy of the knowledge of this subject too.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Good and evil cannot both come from the Lord's mouth, so injustice suffered at evil men's hands is beside his judgment and is loosed in his turning.
comments.comment: … the Lord has not said, nor is cause of the prisoners of the earth being humbled by the sin, nor of human judgments bending opposite God—he loves what is just and straight—nor of a human being becoming worthy to condemn; for the opposites cannot, he says, have come out from the Lord’s mouth, the good things and the evil; for neither does a tree make evil fruits, nor an evil tree good fruits. Being treated unjustly by evil ones, then, is beside the divine judgment, yet it still comes about among those overlooked by God, as happened to the Israelites under the enemies, and in God’s turning it is loosed. For which reason those handed over unto punishment must seek this out (Lamentations 3:38) (Matthew 7:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We murmur in vain against the Creator, for we ourselves are the only cause, so let us judge our own deeds and turn back.
comments.comment: Vainly, then, murmuring we bring the cause up upon the Creator; which the living human being does not have to do; for such a choice belongs to those dead in sins—unless perhaps it convicts the one living according to sin and blaming God. As having, then, no other cause than ourselves alone, having judged the things come about from ourselves let us turn back (Lamentations 3:39–40).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Lifting hearts on hands means examining whether our thoughts are pure.
comments.comment: The taking up of hearts upon hands seems to show that as if having taken our own thoughts in hand let us examine whether they are pure (Lamentations 3:41).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though wronged, he grieves beyond measure for his wrongdoers.
comments.comment: And having suffered so many things he grieves beyond measure for those who have done them—thus “love does not reckon the evil.” (Lamentations 3:48) (1 Corinthians 13:5)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though the eyes were weakened by many tears they did not leave off, and stretched-out prayer and intensified tears draw God to mercy.
comments.comment: Instead of “my eye was worn out, and it will not be silent from there being no sobering,” (Lamentations 3:49) Symmachus said: “my eye persisted, and it did not cease from there being no relief.” And the Seventy show that although the eyes had weakened from a multitude of tears they still were not leaving off—he not being able to sober from the weeping—and Symmachus that I both persisted weeping and was not leaving off; for stretched-out prayer and intensification of tears draws God toward mercy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's weeping and what such persistence does.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Tears cut him down as a vintager cuts a vine, God's looking down means counting us worthy of oversight, and the women's lot is the more pitiable.
comments.comment: For the tears cut me down, he says, just as a precise vintager a vine; and according to Symmachus, that the tears drowned me, by the metaphor of those being choked in waters. And enduring I will endure the Lord, until he turns his face away from us. And God’s peeking-through shows counting us worthy of the oversight. And he interprets the “beyond all” (Lamentations 3:50–51) by bringing it upon all—that is, upon their calamities; for the female gender is more pitiable than that of the males.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God judged, killing the false prophet and handing over the king and the nation.
comments.comment: God judged, having killed the false prophet and having handed over the king, and upon Christ having handed over the nation unto capture. And the “I before their eyes,” (Lamentations 3:58–63) that I was heavy to them even appearing.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The toil given them teaches how great God's shielding was, so that they seek him again.
comments.comment: The “shielding of heart” (Lamentations 3:65–66) is a toil for them, because you will give them a toil unto perception of how great you were when shielding them, so that they may seek you again. And if not, you will chase them in your wrath.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lament is again for the illustrious, whose brilliance has been dimmed.
comments.comment: Beginning the fourth alphabetic sequence now present, he has taken up again especially the lament about the illustrious ones, saying the brilliance has been dimmed and has vanished poured out like water (Lamentations 4:1).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel changed from piety to impiety, as the sons of Zion, precious as gold, were counted as vessels of clay.
comments.comment: … There is indeed a transition occurring from the honorable to the dishonorable; for it has been said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah regarding a great change having happened to Israel from piety to impiety and from practical virtue to practical wickedness: 'the precious sons of Zion, adorned with gold' and silver, 'how they were counted as vessels of clay' (Lamentations 4:2). You see that the precious things are made of gold and silver.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prideful rich and those more honorable than gold were likened to cheap shatterable vessels when led into slavery, as at the potter's house.
comments.comment: Those prideful upon wealth, he says, or even more honorable than gold—how were they so likened to the cheap and shatterable ones, having been led away unto slavery? And he said they were likened to these also when, having gone down into the potter’s house and taking a vessel, he shattered it; and Isaiah also likened them to a city that has fallen, “and its falls will be as shatterings of a vessel.” (Lamentations 4:2) (Jeremiah 18:2–4) (Isaiah 30:14)
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms why the precious sons are compared to clay vessels.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem could not nurse her glorious infants like the wild animals, and the dragons are evil spirits nursing newborns with evil milk.
comments.comment: About famine of the glorious infants he speaks, as Jerusalem not even having been able like the wild animals to hold out a breast to them. And the excess of the passion also works a forgetting of nature. And dragons—or also the Sirens according to Symmachus—you will hear as the evil spirits, those who nursed their own newborns with evil milk. And such are those introduced by the teachings of the impious (Lamentations 4:3).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet likens the supposedly good teachers to Sirens, who destroyed those who met them through pleasure, as dragons inject poison by biting.
comments.comment: For how are they not daughters—those made effeminate, whom Pharaoh also preserves, killing the males? Who also graze upon the teaching, the desert of God, not able like ostriches to fly away, but always running the earth? For “sparrow” (Lamentations 4:3) Symmachus rendered thus, and their teachers he not unfittingly called Sirens. For according to the outer myth these through pleasure were destroying those who met them, just as dragons by biting inject the poison. He reproaches, then, the supposedly good teachers, that not even like these they were eager about those attending (Exodus 1:16–22).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He recalls the captivity, but means a famine of teaching.
comments.comment: Historically he has returned upon the things that happened upon the captivity; but toward the sense he speaks about the famine of the teaching word (Lamentations 4:4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Once nursed on scarlet, they are now rag-clad in earthy thoughts.
comments.comment: Formerly they were being nursed upon scarlet, having heard prophetically beforehand the Savior’s blood about to be poured out, and now being rag-clad from the earthy thoughts (Lamentations 4:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem's lawlessness was greater than Sodom's because she had the written law, the prophets and wonders and sinned against the Savior, while Sodom had only the natural law.
comments.comment: … For what is swifter than a divine word that has said: “behold, your house is left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38) and has handed over by willing alone? And Jerusalem’s lawlessness was magnified beyond that of Sodom. Those had only the natural law; these also a written one and prophets and as many wonders as God was working among them. And those sinned toward angels and toward like human beings; these toward the Savior and redeemer—formerly from Egypt, and now from worship of demons—if they had received the one who came primarily toward them. For “I was not sent,” he says, “except unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” (Matthew 15:24)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Nazirites are those consecrated to God, whose purity is likened to snow, brightness to milk and fired habit to sapphire.
comments.comment: Symmachus: “her unmarked ones set apart than snow, brighter than milk, redder in habit beyond the admired things, sapphire their limbs.” (Lamentations 4:7) He means those who consecrated themselves to God; for “consecrated ones” (Amos 2:11–12) is what Nazirites shows—thus Symmachus and Theodotion in Amos rendered the consecrated ones, having said Nazirites. Moses also mentions these; and such was also Samson. And among Jews they were also eminent. For which reason he compared their purity to snow, and their brightness to milk; and they were fired, having been tested by the askesis of what they were promising to God; and their elect (which is the “fragment”) have a heavenly way of life; for such is sapphire’s color. And it also has goldish veins, to which indeed Symmachus likens their habit, having the incorrupt and the fiery according to piety.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Nazirites fell from spiritual illumination and withered like dry trees, and their faces were blackened with shame.
comments.comment: They fell out of the spiritual illumination and were melted by the intelligible famine, so as to resemble dry woods, those not planted beside the exits of the waters—such as now are the priests among them, not having spiritual good-nourishment. And according to the wording also, their faces were being blackened of extreme shame because sinning like the others they were being led away; since even now upon those being shamed custom has used the name (Lamentations 4:8) (Psalm 1:3).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The women are called compassionate to show that need, not savagery, drove them, as happened in the Romans' siege.
comments.comment: Lest the women seem to have eaten the children through savagery, he says they are compassionate; and he attaches the passion to the necessity of lack. And “they kindled” (Lamentations 4:10) shows the kindling and roasting, which indeed came about upon the Romans’ siege; for which reason he also calls the complete destruction of the nation a shatter. And in the second alphabetic sequence of the Laments he also remembers the present passion. And this and the other passions Josephus has handed down with precision in the things about the capture (Lamentations 2:20).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Starvation is so great an evil that it overpowered both a mother's nature and her will.
comments.comment: [On the starving of the martyr Lucian:] … And so that you may learn how great starvation is, mothers have often tasted their own children, unable to bear the force of this evil. The prophet, lamenting this disaster, said: “The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children” (Lamentations 4:10). Mothers ate the children they bore, and the womb that gave birth became the grave of the children born from it, and starvation overpowered nature—or rather, not nature only, but also the will. …
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what drove the mothers to it.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Completed after Christ.
comments.comment: For after Christ’s sojourn they were completed (Lamentations 4:11).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The just blood is chiefly Christ's, whose shedding destroyed them.
comments.comment: Just blood chiefly is that of the Savior Christ, which having poured out they completely perished, being moderately chastened upon the prophets’ bloods (Lamentations 4:13).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Angels, whom Scripture calls watchers, left the temple, as Josephus records the priests hearing a voice, so that no vision, prophet or leader remained.
comments.comment: Symmachus says: “they became unsettled, blind in the exits, they were stained in blood, so as not to be able to touch their garment.” (Lamentations 4:14) Scripture calls the angels watchers, as in Daniel. And these were those through whom perhaps also the law through Moses was given according to “for if the law spoken through angels.” (Hebrews 2:2) These, then, attending upon her and the divine temple, having been shaken transferred. For Josephus in the things about the capture narrates that “by night the priests, having approached into the sanctuary, as was custom for them toward the liturgies, first said they were perceiving a movement, and after these things a crowded voice: let us transfer from here” (Hebrews 2:2)—when also according to Symmachus they became unsettled and wanderers and blind, he says, in the exits. For there was not a vision distinguishing, not a prophet, nor a leader; for they failed when he came for whom it was laid away, who was expectation of nations (Genesis 49:10).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Kindled' shows the fire of the capture and 'shaken' the transfer into slavery.
comments.comment: And “they were kindled” (Lamentations 4:15) shows the fire of the capture, and “they were shaken” the transfer unto slavery, and “they will not add to sojourn” that they will have a continuous sojourn, no longer needing a second.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's face on the evildoers is punishment from Christ, and the enemies, receiving no priests' face, led all away.
comments.comment: It shows the punishment from Christ; for David says: “the Lord’s face is upon those doing evils.” (Psalm 34:16) And they are not looked upon by him, remaining what they are; for “when the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25) and thereafter as faithful. And if it should be written “their portion,” clearly he says of those going out from the midst. And about the enemies: “they did not receive priests’ face,” (Lamentations 4:16) for they led all away.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The captives repent of leaning on Egypt and Assyria, and believers from the circumcision say the law saves no one.
comments.comment: The word seems to be from the captives, repenting over those on whom they were leaning toward help—Egyptians and Assyrians. And it would also be said consistently by those from the circumcision who believed: we were failing emptily hoping unto the law; for the law saves no one, just as Paul said. Therefore neither will those hanging upon the law be able to help after the grace (Lamentations 4:17) (Galatians 3:11) (Romans 3:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains whose help the captives had watched for in vain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some see Josiah here as a type of Christ, but the spirit before our face is Christ himself, whom those who corrupted their piety seized, and under his shadow the prophets now live among all the nations.
comments.comment:
Some said that among the exceptional ones he more clearly laments Josiah; for they were hoping through his piety for Jerusalem to be raised in the midst of nations unto glory—for Jerusalem is in the midst of nations. And this one, they say, is a type of Christ, having died through the people’s lawlessnesses. And yet he was not seized in the people’s corruptions, but as the prophet forbade, having met Necho Pharaoh, though he was not willing to fight toward him.

According to the divine apostle, then, “a veil lies upon the face of the Jews when Moses is read; but if it turns toward the Lord, the veil is taken around; and the Lord is the spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:17) And through the prophet he calls the Lord spirit. Those, then, upon whom a veil lies would not say: “spirit of our face is Christ the Lord,” (Lamentations 4:20) but those “mirroring the Lord’s glory with uncovered face,” (2 Corinthians 3:18) before whose mind’s eyes the Lord always is; so that clearly the spirit that worked in the prophets was the Christ, who also having become human says: “I myself who speak am present,” (Isaiah 52:6) himself being spirit and Lord and Christ. This one those who first corrupted in themselves the seeds of piety seized. But we the prophets, not considering another the spirit of our face, after our seizure no longer having a place in them, will live under Christ’s shadow—no longer among Jews, but in all the nations—when “the kingdom of God having been lifted from them” (Matthew 21:43) through the daring against Christ “was given to the nations.” (Matthew 21:43) For behold prophets live, speaking about him and proclaiming, but no longer among those who still even now surround him with their own corruptions, blaspheming him daily.

And Aquila said “spirit of our nostrils,” and Symmachus “breath of our nostrils.” For the God-loving continually breathe Christ, having him before the eyes. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the anointed is, how he was taken, and what living under his shadow among the nations means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteous now have Christ the life only in a shadow, and if the shadow gave the prophets such goods, life in the life itself will be far greater.
comments.comment: This life is Christ, who said, I am the life. This life which now is present to the righteous in a shadow, but then face to face. For the spirit before our face is Christ the Lord, of whom we said: In his shadow we shall live among the nations. If your shadow of the life grants such goods — such as Moses had when prophesying, such as Isaiah had when seeing the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a throne high and lifted up, … — such as Ezekiel had when seeing the cherubim, seeing the wheels, the unspeakable mysteries — how shall we live when we no longer live under the shadow of the life, but come to be in the life itself …?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to live under his shadow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ gave the spirit of prophecy and the law is his shadow, or else believers say they will live in his shadow by imitating him.
comments.comment: … And you would say “spirit of face is Christ,” the one who gifted us the spirit of prophecy; for this is prophets’ face, and spirit the gift, and shadow the law—“for the law having a shadow of the good things about to be.” (Hebrews 10:1) The prophets, then, lived among us and in the law’s shadow. The prophetic gift, then, toward which the outcome of all prophecy looks, is Christ—that is, from Christ. “For Christ is end of law and prophets.” (Romans 10:4) And it would also be said from the apostles’ and believers’ person; “for in him we both live and move and are” (Hebrews 10:1); of whom we said “in his shadow we will live,” that is according to imitation of him. For the divine apostle says: “become imitators of me just as I also of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The word is against Edom, Esau's line, who kept ancestral hatred toward Jacob, and foretells an excess of evils that Christ will bring on the Earthly.
comments.comment: The word is toward those from Edom and Esau the brother of Jacob, foretelling an excess of evils for them (for this is the “you will be drunk and you will pour out” (Lamentations 4:21)), about whom David also says: “remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, those saying: empty, empty, until the foundation in it.” (Psalm 137:7) For being brothers and neighbors, they preserved the ancestral hate. And having spoken about Christ unto a season he also remembered this. For Christ was about to sack the one called Earthly, working a heavenly. For virtue and knowledge are threatening toward those who love errors and passions—whose drunkenness is the death of the flesh, and over-outpouring also the putting-to-death of its mindset (Romans 8:6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God will not add to the captivity, since he lessens the penalty, and the word may refer to the last captivity, after which all Israel will be saved.
comments.comment: You have paid a sufficient penalty, in which Edom will succeed. And the “he will not add to relocate you” (Lamentations 4:22) either speaks toward the recalling—for you will not remain upon the captivity, having filled the complete measure; for God lessens the penalty, he does not add—or if it has been said toward a second capture as not about to come to be, how did the one after that under Romans come to be? Perhaps, then, the word is about the last one that came to be because of Christ, after which another has not come to be. And all Israel will be saved after the fullness of the nations, having left the lawlessness; after which thereafter the completion, and the punishment of the earthly things, the judgment receiving. And the word would also be said toward the church, which is daughter of the synagogue of old (“for the gifts of God are without regret,” and her lawlessness failed through the divine baptism), which he no longer hands over to the enemies who said: “here I will dwell, because I chose her” and “behold I am with you all the days until the completion of the age” (Matthew 28:20)—when he also pilloried the impiety of those who mind the earthly things (Philippians 3:19).
comments.selected_reason: Asks what 'no more carry thee away' means and answers it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
